presentingComplaint: Facial rash, joint pains, and frothy urine for 3 weeks, with worsening fatigue and low-grade fever
history: A 27-year-old woman with SLE diagnosed 4 years ago (previously well-controlled on hydroxychloroquine, now non-adherent for the past 3 months due to financial constraints) presents with a 3-week history of worsening malar rash, symmetric small-joint pain and swelling in the hands and wrists, low-grade fevers, and increasing fatigue. Over the last 10 days she has noticed frothy, bubbly urine and bilateral ankle swelling. She denies dysuria, hematuria visible to the naked eye, chest pain, or shortness of breath. No recent infections, new medications, or excessive sun exposure reported, though she did attend an outdoor wedding 4 weeks ago. She has had increased hair shedding and two painless oral ulcers over the past week. No history of seizures, psychosis, or focal neurological symptoms.
examination: Malar (butterfly) rash sparing the nasolabial folds, healed discoid-type scarring on the scalp with patchy alopecia, one small painless ulcer on the hard palate. Bilateral pitting edema of the ankles to mid-shin. Symmetric synovitis and tenderness of the MCP and PIP joints of both hands and wrists without deformity. No oral candidiasis. Chest clear to auscultation, no pericardial rub. Abdomen soft, non-tender, no organomegaly. No focal neurological deficits; alert and oriented.

labs.urinalysis: 3+ protein, dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts, few WBCs, no nitrites
labs.urineMicroscopy: active sediment with dysmorphic RBCs and RBC casts

imaging: Renal ultrasound: normal-sized kidneys, preserved corticomedullary differentiation, no obstruction
Chest X-ray: no infiltrate or effusion
Hand X-rays: soft tissue swelling only, no erosions
microbiology: HIV, hepatitis B and C serologies: negative
finalDiagnosis: Systemic lupus erythematosus flare with active lupus nephritis (multisystem: mucocutaneous, articular, hematologic, renal)
citations: EULAR Recommendations for Management of SLE 2019
contraindications: Avoid live vaccines if escalating immunosuppression (e.g., high-dose steroids, mycophenolate, cyclophosphamide)
Screen for TB and hepatitis B before starting biologics or heavy immunosuppression
Confirm G6PD status not required for hydroxychloroquine but check baseline ophthalmologic exam before continuing
Avoid nephrotoxic agents (e.g., contrast, aminoglycosides) given active nephritis
edgeCases: Cytopenias (leukopenia, lymphopenia, mild thrombocytopenia) with a positive but non-hemolyzing Coombs test can mimic TTP/HUS or hematologic malignancy — schistocytes on smear and ADAMTS13 help exclude TMA

Active urine sediment with rising creatinine mandates renal biopsy to classify lupus nephritis class and guide induction therapy (not modeled as a distinct engine id — case is captured under 'sle_flare')
Non-adherence to hydroxychloroquine is a common precipitant of flare and should be addressed alongside acute management

Because 'lupus nephritis' is not a separate id in the diagnosable list, the overall flare with renal involvement is best captured as sle_flare; acceptableIds intentionally excludes a separate nephritis-specific id
expectedMaiK: MaiK should flag multisystem lupus flare with renal involvement (active urinary sediment, rising creatinine, hypocomplementemia, high anti-dsDNA) as requiring urgent nephrology referral and renal biopsy to guide immunosuppressive induction; this is a non-infective rheumatologic emergency, not a sepsis/infection pathway.
